To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have generated a novel genetic tool to study the role of G protein-coupling in specific cell types and that this tool revealed that the GPCR, 3-iodothyonamine, regulates insulin secretion in pancreatic beta cells via G(i)-coupling and that this pathway may be relevant to physiological control of glucose metabolism in vivo.

(1) we generated a new mouse line to achieve tissue-specific inhibition of G(i/o)/G(s) signaling in vivo, (2) we used this mouse line to identify G(i/o)- and G(s)-coupling of 3-iodo-thyronine and protease- activated receptor 2 to insulin secretion, and (3) we found that the G(i/o)-inhibited mouse line is protected against diet-induced obesity.
1) We have developed a new genetic tool, the ROSA26( PTX) mouse, that allows the study of G(i/o), and hence GPCRs, in vivo in a cell type-specific manner.

the role of the GPCR signaling pathway in the regulation of insulin secretion and the role of specific GPCR in the control of glucose homeostasis.
understanding the function and regulation of GPCRs, which is a fundamental problem in biology and medicine.
the role of GPCRs in the regulation of glucose metabolism and insulin secretion.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we used the ROSA26(crePTX) system to show the importance of Gi/o signaling for insulin secretion, identified the Gi/o-coupled receptors expressed in islets, and used these receptors as a starting point to identify novel regulators of insulin secretion.
the ROSA26( PTX) mouse system is a new genetic tool that can be applied for tissue-specific inhibition of GPCR signaling.
we have developed a genetic tool that allows for tissue-specific modulation of G protein signaling in vivo and used this tool to investigate the roles of G(i) signaling in pancreatic beta cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the ROSA26(CT2-PTX) mouse is an effective tool to investigate in vivo the functions of G(i/o)/G(s) coupled GPCRs in a variety of cell types, and in this work we have used it to show that GPCRs regulate insulin secretion in pancreatic beta cells.
the G(i) subunit is important in the regulation of insulin secretion and that G(i)-coupling of GPCRs is an underappreciated regulator of glucose metabolism.
the ROSA26(CT) and ROSA26(ET) alleles can be used to generate tissue-specific pertussis toxin transgenic mice.
